title: Le Blanc: freedom is formally neither in intellect nor will but in the man acting through both
source_text: XLVI. Sed mihi potius dicendum videtur neque in intellectu, neque in voluntate libertatem esse formaliter, sed in homine quatenus per intellectum & voluntatem agit. Siquidem libertas proprie loquendo, non est affectio hujus, aut illius facultatis, sed aliquid oriens ex plurium facultatum relatione mutua & concursu; & quod proinde nulli certae facultati proprie attribui potest, sed solum supposito in quo facultates illae reperiuntur. Itaque si exacte loquamur, nec mens, nec voluntas liberae dicendae sunt, sed homo ipse quatenus facultatibus illis certo modo utitur. Quum vero voluntas libera vocatur, enunciatio non est, ut Scholae loquuntur, formalis, sed causalis: quia, scilicet, voluntas intellectui juncta, causa est actionum, quarum respectu homo libere agere dicitur. Quae observatio non est omnino de nihilo, ut in sequentibus videri poterit. Facit enim ad solvendas quasdam difficultates quibus se implicant non pauci, dum totam libertatis rationem in voluntate, non simpliciter in homine quaerunt.
pass_a_gloss: But to me it seems rather to be said that liberty is formally neither in the intellect, nor in the will, but in man inasmuch as he acts through intellect & will. Since liberty properly speaking, is not an affection of this, or that faculty, but something arising from the mutual relation & concourse of several faculties; & which therefore cannot properly be attributed to any certain faculty, but only to the suppositum in which those faculties are found. Therefore if we speak exactly, neither the mind, nor the will are to be called free, but man himself inasmuch as he uses those faculties in a certain way. But when the will is called free, the enunciation is not, as the Schools speak, formal, but causal: because, namely, the will joined to the intellect, is the cause of the actions, in respect of which man is said to act freely. Which observation is not altogether of nothing, as can be seen in what follows. For it serves to solve certain difficulties in which not a few entangle themselves, while they seek the whole account of liberty in the will, not simply in man.
pass_b_english: My own view is rather that freedom is formally neither in the intellect nor in the will, but in man as he acts through intellect and will. Freedom, properly speaking, is not a disposition of this faculty or that. It arises from the mutual relation and joint working of several faculties, and so it cannot properly be ascribed to any one faculty, only to the subject (suppositum) in which those faculties are found.

Strictly speaking, then, neither mind nor will should be called free, but man himself, in so far as he uses those faculties in a certain way. When the will is called free, the statement is not, in the language of the schools, formal but causal: the will, joined to the intellect, is the cause of the actions for which man is said to act freely.

This point is not idle, as will appear later. It helps to resolve certain difficulties in which a good many entangle themselves by looking for the whole nature of freedom in the will rather than in the man as such.

choices.why: Suppositum is the scholastic term for the concrete individual that has the faculties; the Latin is kept in brackets.
